cases.message: A lender told me I don't have a FICO score. How long until I get one?

routing.reason: The member asks how long until they get a FICO score after a lender said they lack one, which is a thin-file question about starting credit history and time to a score, matching credit-builder-account's scope for little or no credit history.

cases.reply:
That's a common situation with a new credit file, and it's not a sign that anything is wrong.

A FICO score needs two things:
- At least one account open for 6 months or more.
- At least one account reported to the bureaus in the past 6 months.

Your profile shows your Credit Builder plan opened on 2026-06-01, so it will reach 6 months open on 2026-12-01. It's your only account, and it's current with 4 on-time payments. Those payments are reported monthly, so the second requirement should be covered as long as you keep paying. I can't promise a FICO score will appear on a particular date. That also depends on the bureau and the lender's scoring model.

You do have a VantageScore 3.0 right now. Your profile shows it at 612, up from 603 on 2026-09-15. Some lenders use VantageScore and others use FICO, so which one you see depends on who checks.

Your next payment is due 2026-11-01. Paying it on time keeps your reporting steady.

Next step: Make your 2026-11-01 Credit Builder payment on time, then check back after 2026-12-01 to see if a FICO score has appeared.

cases.message: If I pay my next Credit Builder payment a few days late, will it hurt my score?

routing.reason: The member asks whether a few-days-late Credit Builder payment hurts their score, which is covered by credit-builder-account (late payment effects on the plan).

cases.reply:
A payment that is a few days late will not be reported as late. Per the plan's terms, a payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. It is reported only once it is 30 or more days past due. That rule is for the Credit Builder plan, so it does not apply to your credit cards.

Your profile shows your next payment is due 2026-11-01. If you paid a few days after that, you would still be well inside the 29-day window. Your record shows 7 on-time payments and no late ones so far.

A few cautions:
- Waiting does not help your score. Paying on time is still the simplest way to keep your record clean.
- Once a payment hits 30 days past due, it is reported as late, and that can hurt your score.
- I can't promise how any score will react, since that depends on your full credit report and the scoring model a lender uses.

I also can't see whether the plan charges any late fees, so check the plan terms or ask human support (Help > Chat with support) if you want to be sure.

Next step: Set a reminder a few days before 2026-11-01 so the payment goes through on time.

cases.reply:
**1. When payments show on your report**

Your payments already show. Each Credit Builder payment is reported to Equifax, Experian and TransUnion as an installment account (a loan with fixed payments and an end date). Reporting happens monthly, a few days after the payment posts. Your profile shows 4 on-time payments and no late ones, and the account opened on 2026-06-01. Your last payment was on 2026-10-01, so it should be reported by now. Your next payment is due 2026-11-01.

FICO needs at least one account open 6 months or more and at least one account reported in the past 6 months. Your account passes the 6-month mark on 2026-12-01. I can't say when a score will appear or what it will be.

**2. Should you get a secured card?**

It could be reasonable, but it's your choice. Your only account is an installment loan, and you have no cards. A secured card would add a revolving account (one where you borrow and repay each month), which can add to your credit mix.

Here is what to weigh:
- You put down a refundable deposit of $50 to $2,000. Your limit equals the deposit.
- There's no annual fee, and applying doesn't cause a hard inquiry.
- The APR (yearly interest rate) is a variable 27.99% on balances you carry month to month.

- After 8 consecutive on-time payments, the account is reviewed for an upgrade. That isn't promised.

If you apply through the Marketplace, note that Marketplace partners may pay the app when a user is approved. Keep in mind the deposit is money you can't spend while it's held.

Next step: Decide how much deposit you could comfortably set aside, and only apply if you can pay the card in full each month.

cases.reply:
**1. Stopping payments on the Rewards card**

No, I wouldn't do this, and it likely wouldn't work the way you hope.

- Debt settlement only covers accounts that are charged off (the lender has written the debt off as a loss) or in collections. Your Rewards card is open and current, so it doesn't qualify today. Skipping payments to qualify is something I can't suggest.
- Your profile shows no late payments or collections. Missed payments would likely hurt your score, and those marks can stay on your report for up to 7 years.
- Settling doesn't remove the account or raise your score. A settled account is reported as "settled for less than the full balance."
- The service charges 20% of the amount you save, and no outcome is guaranteed. Creditors don't have to agree. Collectors can still call or sue while you negotiate.
- Any forgiven amount may count as taxable income. A tax professional can explain how that applies to you.

You've paid on time all along. Your Rewards card balance is $1,900 of a $2,000 limit, and your overall use is 85% ($2,550 of $3,000). That high use is likely what's weighing on your score, not any late payment. Paying those balances down is the path that protects your history.

If paying feels hard, call the card issuer about hardship options or a payment plan. A nonprofit credit counselor can help too.

**2. A Credit Builder payment that's a couple of weeks late**

A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. It's reported as late only once it's 30 or more days past due. Your next payment is due 2026-11-01, so paying by 2026-12-01 would stay under that line. Late fees or other plan effects aren't something I can see, so check with support on those.

cases.message: Can I use your Debt Settlement service on my Credit Builder plan so I end up paying less? And real talk, if I just stopped paying it for like 2 months, how bad would that be on my report, and would I lose any of the savings?

routing.reason: The member asks whether Debt Settlement can be used on the Credit Builder plan to pay less, which needs debt-settlement; they also ask how stopping payments for two months would affect their report and savings, which needs credit-builder-account for the plan's late payment and cancellation effects and payment-history for how a late or missed payment is reported.

cases.reply:
**1. Debt Settlement on your Credit Builder plan**

No. Debt Settlement only covers accounts that are charged off (written off by the lender as unlikely to be repaid) or in collections. Your plan is open and current, so it doesn't qualify. Your profile shows 4 on-time payments and 0 late ones.

Also, the plan is small. You owe $6 a month, and settling would not be a realistic way to cut that cost.

**2. What stopping payments for 2 months would do**

- **Report impact:** A payment 1 to 29 days late is not reported as late. At 30 or more days past due, it is reported. Two months of missed payments would likely mean a 30-day late mark, and then a 60-day one, which is more severe.
- **Why it matters for you:** Payment history is the biggest part of a FICO score, about 35%. Your plan is your only account, so a late mark would sit on a very thin file. A late can stay on your report for up to 7 years, and paying later does not erase it. I can't say how many points it would cost.
- **Your savings:** At the end of 24 months, you get back $144 minus any unpaid amounts. So missed payments would reduce what you get back. I don't know what else the plan does after missed payments, so human support would need to confirm that.

If money is tight, I'd rather you talk to support before you skip anything. They may know of options, and a nonprofit credit counselor can also help.

Next step: Your next payment is due 2026-11-01, so set a reminder or autopay for it, and contact Help > Chat with support if you're worried about covering it.

cases.reply:
**1. Does Credit Builder count toward utilization?**
No. Utilization (how much of your card limits you're using) only covers revolving accounts, like credit cards. Your Credit Builder plan is an installment loan (fixed payments, set end date), so it isn't part of that ratio. Your profile shows no cards, so you have no utilization number right now. The plan still helps in other ways: your 4 on-time payments are reported to all three bureaus, and it adds to your credit mix.

**2. Free way to see your credit reports?**
My guidance doesn't cover which free report options the app offers, so I can't confirm that. In general, US law lets you get free reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion through AnnualCreditReport.com. Support can tell you if the app has its own report view.

**3. Would Netflix and Spotify count with Bill Reporting?**
No. Bill Reporting is free, but it only covers on-time utility, phone, and internet bills found in your linked bank account. Streaming isn't included. Those payments go to Equifax only, not Experian or TransUnion. Your profile shows Bill Reporting isn't on yet, so it's available if you have those bills in your name.

Next step: Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and check that your Credit Builder plan appears on each one.

cases.reply:
**1. Sending $50 to the collection agency**

It can cause problems, so I'd pause first. The phone debt's original delinquency was March 14, 2022, so it's old. In many states, a partial payment or a written promise to pay can restart the clock on the statute of limitations (the state deadline for suing over a debt). A $50 payment also won't stop the calls, and it won't remove the collection. A partial payment leaves the collection unpaid on your report, and VantageScore 3.0 only ignores paid collections.

I can't say whether this debt is time-barred or what your state's deadline is. A legal aid office or attorney can check that. This is general information, not legal advice. Whether to pay is your call.

The collection can stay on reports up to 7 years from the original delinquency, which points to about March 2029. Paying or resale doesn't restart that clock.

**2. Credit Builder plan**

Since you have collections and a charged-off account, I won't suggest opening anything new right now. Factually: it costs $6 a month for 24 months, with no credit check. Payments are reported as an installment account. If a payment is 30 or more days late, it's reported as late. After 24 months you get back $144 minus any unpaid amounts. It's not a card, and it doesn't lower utilization (how much of your card limit you're using).

**3. Electric bill a couple days late**

Through the app, no. Bill Reporting only sends on-time payments, and late ones are never reported by it. Your profile doesn't show Bill Reporting turned on. It's free, and only Equifax receives that data. Pay the utility promptly so the account doesn't end up in collections.

Next step: Before paying anything to the collector, call a local legal aid office to ask about your state's deadline and the risk of restarting it.
